raw:
These hypotheses come from my prior knowledge of NAS-Bench-201 behavior; I did not run any queries against the benchmark. The main structural facts I relied on:

- Convolutions on the direct input-to-output path (edge 3) matter a lot.
- Edges that feed the output node (3, 4, 5) matter most.
- If a path is already disconnected or weak, a new op adds more.
- Conv ops add the most when the competing paths are only skip or pool.

1. Setting edge 4 (1→3) to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 3 (0→3) is none. Without the direct path, the conv on edge 4 becomes more important.
2. Setting edge 5 (2→3) to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 3 is none, for the same reason.
3. Setting edge 3 to nor_conv_3x3 helps less when edge 3 currently holds nor_conv_1x1, because it replaces a conv with a similar op, so the gain is small compared with replacing none.
4. Setting edge 0 (0→1) to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 4 is nor_conv_3x3, because edge 0 is only useful if node 1 is passed on to the output.
5. Setting edge 0 to nor_conv_3x3 helps less when edge 4 is none and edge 2 is none, since node 1 is then a dead end. I use edge 4 = none as the condition, so the direction is "lower".
6. Setting edge 3 to skip_connect helps more when edge 5 is none, since a skip supplies a gradient path when the others are cut.
7. Setting edge 1 (0→2) to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 5 is nor_conv_3x3, because node 2 then feeds the output through a conv.
8. Setting edge 5 to none hurts less (higher effect) when edge 3 is nor_conv_3x3, because a strong direct path makes edge 5 redundant.
9. Setting edge 2 (1→2) to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 5 is nor_conv_3x3, because edge 2 matters only if node 2 flows onward.
10. Setting edge 4 to avg_pool_3x3 has a higher effect when edge 4 currently holds none than when it holds a conv. Replacing a conv with pooling is a loss, while adding pooling over none is not.
